corrected_value.title: Sympathy and callousness: The impact of deliberative thought on donations to identifiable and statistical victims

decisions.quote:
We conducted
                    a pre-registered far replication and extension of Studies 1 and 3 in Small et al. (2007), a
                    seminal demonstration of the identifiable victim effect, with hypothetical donations. We
                    examined the impact of deliberative thinking on the identifiable victim effect both by
                    directly informing participants of the effect (Study 1) and by providing an identified
                    victim with statistical information (Study 3).
decisions.reason: Both the shipped record and blind coding identify Small, Loewenstein, and Slovic (2007) (DOI: 10.1016/j.obhdp.2006.01.005) as the target original study whose Studies 1 and 3 are re-tested in a unified experimental design.

decisions.quote:
We conducted a replication and extension of Small et
al. (2007) with modified setting and using hypothetical do-
nations. Contrary to the target article’s findings, we did
not find support for the identifiable victim effect and did
not find support for explicit and implicit interventions as
weakening the effect.
decisions.reason: The authors state an explicit overall verdict that contrary to Small et al. (2007), their high-powered replication (N = 1,004) found no support for the identifiable victim effect (H1a) and no support for explicit learning (H2a, H3a) or implicit learning/joint presentation (H4) weakening the effect, nor for differential correlation between aggregated feelings and donations across conditions (summarizing all replication comparisons in Table 11 as 'No signal - inconsistent'). Their discussion of hypothetical versus real donations notes a boundary on generalizability rather than declaring the study uninformative, and the perceived-impact finding (H6) is explicitly an extension.
